episode_title: Why Smart People Make Bad Decisions (#326)

real_qa.q: Why did Israeli daycare centers see parents arrive even later after implementing a fine for late pickups?
real_qa.r: The daycare centers instituted a small fine (equivalent to three or five dollars) for late pickups. This transformed what was previously an obligation or duty into a transaction with a price. Parents who used to feel guilty about being late now saw it as a small fee they could afford to pay, so some decided to stay longer at activities like tennis, knowing they could simply pay the fine. As Dubner explains: if the price is too low, it can encourage the wrong kind of behavior.
real_qa.requete: Israeli daycare late pickup fine unintended consequences

real_qa.q: What is the cobra effect and how does it demonstrate unintended consequences?
real_qa.r: The cobra effect originated in colonial India when a bounty was placed on cobras: people received money for turning in the tail of a dead cobra. Rather than reducing the cobra population, people responded by breeding, raising, and killing extra cobras specifically to claim the reward. This is a classic example of how putting a price on eliminating a problem can perversely incentivize people to create more of that problem.
real_qa.requete: cobra effect bounty unintended consequences definition

real_qa.q: How did Chicago public school teachers cheat on No Child Left Behind tests and what did this reveal?
real_qa.r: Under the No Child Left Behind federal education legislation, teachers who faced financial incentives tied to student performance engaged in cheating by literally erasing wrong answers on bubble tests and filling in correct ones. Dubner notes that patterns in test data revealed this—for example, students getting easier questions wrong but harder questions perfectly right. Most disturbingly, the teachers most likely to cheat were the worst teachers, those with many failing students, meaning they were helping themselves rather than truly helping their students.
real_qa.requete: Chicago teachers cheating No Child Left Behind bubble tests

real_qa.q: What does Stephen Dubner say is the wrong question about artificial intelligence?
real_qa.r: Dubner argues that the wrong question is 'When will AI kill us?' and the right question is 'What can we do with AI?' He contends that people consistently get the story of new technology wrong in its early days, with evangelists exaggerating benefits and naysayers expressing unfounded fears—a pattern he sees throughout history, including fears about electricity itself.
real_qa.requete: Stephen Dubner wrong question about AI artificial intelligence

real_qa.q: What is the relationship between improved medical treatments for heart disease and rising cancer death rates?
real_qa.r: Dubner explains that because medical advances have been so effective at treating heart disease, more people now survive long enough to develop and die from cancer—a disease they would have died from heart disease to avoid two decades earlier. He uses his own father as an example, noting that conditions like hypertension and stroke that killed his father at 56 are now preventable or treatable in the modern era, representing genuine progress even if cancer remains a challenge.
real_qa.requete: heart disease treatment cancer death rate unintended consequences
